claim: Human organoid systems recapitulate key features of organs offering platforms for modelling developmental biology and disease.
source: Human organoid systems recapitulate key features of organs offering platforms for modelling developmental biology and disease.
evidence: This is a general statement about organoid systems supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Tissue-derived organoids have been widely used to study the impact of extrinsic niche factors on stem cells.
source: Tissue-derived organoids have been widely used to study the impact of extrinsic niche factors on stem cells.
evidence: This statement reflects established use of tissue-derived organoids in the field.

claim: Tissue-derived organoids are rarely used to study endogenous gene function due to the lack of efficient gene manipulation tools.
source: However, they are rarely used to study endogenous gene function due to the lack of efficient gene manipulation tools.
evidence: This is an assertion about the current state of the field that motivates the study.

claim: A human foetal lung organoid system was previously established by Nikolić et al., 2017.
source: Previously, we established a human foetal lung organoid system (Nikolić et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: The authors have systematically developed and optimised a complete genetic toolbox for use in tissue-derived organoids using the human foetal lung organoid system.
source: Here, using this organoid system as an example, we have systematically developed and optimised a complete genetic toolbox for use in tissue-derived organoids.
evidence: This is the main claim of the manuscript, supported by the experimental data presented throughout.

claim: 'Organoid Easytag' is an efficient workflow for targeting all types of gene loci through CRISPR-mediated homologous recombination followed by flow cytometry for enriching correctly targeted cells.
source: This includes 'Organoid Easytag', our efficient workflow for targeting all types of gene loci through CRISPR-mediated homologous recombination followed by flow cytometry for enriching correctly targeted cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing successful gene targeting in multiple loci.

claim: The toolbox incorporates conditional gene knockdown or overexpression using tightly inducible CRISPR interference and CRISPR activation.
source: Our toolbox also incorporates conditional gene knockdown or overexpression using tightly inducible CRISPR interference and CRISPR activation which is the first efficient application of these techniques to tissue-derived organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing CRISPRi and CRISPRa functionality in organoids.

claim: This is the first efficient application of CRISPR interference and CRISPR activation techniques to tissue-derived organoids.
source: Our toolbox also incorporates conditional gene knockdown or overexpression using tightly inducible CRISPR interference and CRISPR activation which is the first efficient application of these techniques to tissue-derived organoids.
evidence: This is a claim about novelty in the field, based on the authors' knowledge of existing literature.

claim: CRISPR and its related techniques have been rapidly adopted in cancer and pluripotent stem cell lines.
source: They have been rapidly adopted in cancer and pluripotent stem cell (PSC) lines (Bowden et al., 2020; Gilbert et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2019), but not in tissue-derived human organoids.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CRISPR and its related techniques have not been adopted in tissue-derived human organoids.
source: They have been rapidly adopted in cancer and pluripotent stem cell (PSC) lines (Bowden et al., 2020; Gilbert et al., 2013; Tian et al., 2019), but not in tissue-derived human organoids.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the field that motivates the study.

claim: A recent application of non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) to improve gene targeting in organoids has been successful.
source: A recent application of non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) to improve gene targeting in organoids has been successful (Artegiani et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The authors adopted a homology-directed repair (HDR) strategy as a complementary approach to NHEJ.
source: However, we adopted a homology-directed repair (HDR) strategy as a complementary approach.
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors.

claim: The recombination-based HDR method allows precise genetic manipulation with flexible targeting sites and minimal additional genetic changes.
source: We reasoned that the recombination-based method allows our strategy to deliver precise genetic manipulation with flexible targeting sites and minimal additional genetic changes.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the advantages of HDR, based on established knowledge of the technique.

claim: Nucleofection achieved up to 70% transfection efficiency in organoid cells.
source: Nucleofection achieved up to 70% transfection efficiency and showed consistency across different organoid lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Nucleofection showed consistency across different organoid lines.
source: Nucleofection achieved up to 70% transfection efficiency and showed consistency across different organoid lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: Cas9 ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) outperformed plasmid-based Cas9 approaches in both the T7 endonuclease assay and an online CRISPR editing analysis tool.
source: Consistent with previous reports, Cas9 ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) outperformed plasmid-based Cas9 approaches (Kim et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2014), both in the T7 endonuclease assay and an online CRISPR editing analysis tool (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The RNP strategy has the advantage that the RNP is rapidly degraded and should produce minimal off-target effects.
source: This strategy has the advantage that the RNP is rapidly degraded and should produce minimal off-target effects.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the advantages of RNPs, based on established knowledge and speculation about off-target effects.

claim: β-actin (ACTB) protein is abundant in human foetal lung organoids.
source: To establish our gene targeting workflow, we first focused on generating a β-actin (ACTB)-fusion protein, taking advantage of the abundance of ACTB protein in human foetal lung organoids and a previously published targeting strategy (Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation about ACTB expression in the organoid system.

claim: 72 hr after nucleofection of the ssRNP and repair template, mEGFP+ organoid cells could be enriched by flow cytometry.
source: As expected, 72 hr after nucleofection of the ssRNP and repair template, mEGFP+ organoid cells could be enriched by flow cytometry (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: 59% of organoid lines (n = 17/29 lines, from N = 2 parental organoid lines) were correctly targeted for mEGFP-ACTB.
source: These small colonies could be further expanded into new organoid lines and 59% of lines (n = 17/29 lines, from N = 2 parental organoid lines, Supplementary file 1) were correctly targeted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantifying targeting efficiency.

claim: The mEGFP-ACTB fusion protein localised to cell–cell junctions.
source: The mEGFP-ACTB fusion protein localised to cell–cell junctions as expected (Roberts et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Targeted organoids continued to express the multipotent lung progenitor marker, SOX9.
source: Targeted organoids continued to express the multipotent lung progenitor marker, SOX9 (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: None of the HDR-enhancing drugs tested increased the rate of gene targeting.
source: However, using flow cytometry as a simple assay, none of the drugs tested increased the rate of gene targeting (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The AAVS1 locus has been considered to be a 'safe harbour locus' for expressing exogenous genes in a controllable manner in human cells without silencing.
source: The AAVS1 locus (Adeno-Associated Virus Integration Site 1, located in the first intron of the PPP1R12C gene) has been considered to be a 'safe harbour locus' for expressing exogenous genes in a controllable manner in human cells without silencing (Smith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The authors successfully targeted AAVS1 to express a membrane tagged TagRFP-T (mTagRFP-T) for cell shape visualisation (n = 4/6 correctly targeted lines from N = 1 parental organoid line).
source: As a further proof of concept, we successfully targeted AAVS1 to express a membrane tagged TagRFP-T (mTagRFP-T) for cell shape visualisation (Figure 1f and g; n = 4/6 correctly targeted lines from N = 1 parental organoid line).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: SOX9 is a transcription factor and a tip progenitor cell marker for developing lungs.
source: SOX9, a transcription factor, is a tip progenitor cell marker for developing lungs (Nikolić et al., 2017), and SOX9 reporters are useful for monitoring organoid progenitor state.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SOX9 reporters are useful for monitoring organoid progenitor state.
source: SOX9, a transcription factor, is a tip progenitor cell marker for developing lungs (Nikolić et al., 2017), and SOX9 reporters are useful for monitoring organoid progenitor state.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the utility of SOX9 reporters.

claim: A Histone H2B-EGFP fusion (H2B-EGFP) was used to concentrate the EGFP signal in the nucleus to overcome SOX9's low expression level.
source: To overcome its low expression level, we used a Histone H2B-EGFP fusion (H2B-EGFP hereafter) to concentrate the EGFP signal in the nucleus (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a methodological strategy described by the authors.

claim: A T2A sequence was inserted between SOX9 and H2B-EGFP to ensure that SOX9 protein was minimally influenced.
source: A T2A sequence, a self-cleavage peptide, was also inserted between SOX9 and H2B-EGFP to ensure that SOX9 protein was minimally influenced.
evidence: This is a methodological strategy described by the authors.

claim: 9 out of 23 SOX9 reporter lines from 3 parental organoid lines were correctly targeted.
source: Targeted colonies could be expanded and maintained normal SOX2, SOX9 and NKX2-1 expression (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a; n = 9/23 correctly targeted lines from N = 3 parental organoid lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data quantifying targeting efficiency.

claim: SOX9 reporter organoids maintained normal SOX2, SOX9 and NKX2-1 expression.
source: Targeted colonies could be expanded and maintained normal SOX2, SOX9 and NKX2-1 expression (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a; n = 9/23 correctly targeted lines from N = 3 parental organoid lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The authors were only able to generate SOX9 reporter lines as heterozygotes.
source: Importantly, we noted that although we were only able to generate SOX9 reporter lines as heterozygotes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c), the gRNA sites in the wildtype alleles were intact (6/6 lines tested, N = 3 parental organoid lines) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by genotyping data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The gRNA sites in the wildtype alleles of SOX9 reporter heterozygotes were intact (6/6 lines tested, N = 3 parental organoid lines).
source: Importantly, we noted that although we were only able to generate SOX9 reporter lines as heterozygotes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and c), the gRNA sites in the wildtype alleles were intact (6/6 lines tested, N = 3 parental organoid lines) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: No indels were detected within ~200 bps flanking the top nine most probable SOX9 gRNA off-target sites in 3/3 SOX9-T2A-H2B-EGFP lines tested.
source: No indels were detected within ~200 bps flanking these potential off-target sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e and f), suggesting low off-target effects of our workflow (3/3 SOX9-T2A-H2B-EGFP lines tested).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The low off-target effects suggest that the Organoid Easytag workflow has minimal off-target effects.
source: No indels were detected within ~200 bps flanking these potential off-target sites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e and f), suggesting low off-target effects of our workflow (3/3 SOX9-T2A-H2B-EGFP lines tested).
evidence: This is an inference based on the off-target analysis data.

claim: SOX9-targeted organoids retained the potential to differentiate.
source: Additionally, we validated that the SOX9-targeted organoids retained the potential to differentiate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g), further demonstrating the normality of the targeted organoid lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by differentiation assay data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The generation of straightforward gene KOs by induction of indels using the CRISPR-Cas9 system can suffer from translation retention and exon skipping.
source: The generation of straightforward gene KOs by induction of indels using the CRISPR-Cas9 system can suffer from translation retention and exon skipping (Smits et al., 2019; Tuladhar et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The authors replaced the SOX2 coding sequence (CDS) with T2A-H2B-EGFP to generate SOX2 KO organoids.
source: We replaced the SOX2 coding sequence (CDS) with T2A-H2B-EGFP to generate SOX2 KO organoids.
evidence: This is a methodological approach described by the authors.

claim: The authors sequentially replaced both copies of the SOX2 CDS using two gRNAs targeting the N and C terminal of the SOX2 CDS.
source: Using two gRNAs targeting the N and C terminal of the SOX2 CDS, respectively, we sequentially replaced both copies of the SOX2 CDS (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The EGFP signal was increased after targeting the second copy of the SOX2 CDS.
source: The EGFP signal was increased after targeting the second copy of the SOX2 CDS, making selection of serially targeted alleles by flow cytometry straightforward (Figure 2—figure supplement 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: SOX2 KO colonies proliferate and grow normally for at least four serial passages.
source: SOX2 KO colonies proliferate and grow normally for at least four serial passages, suggesting that SOX2 is not crucial for human foetal lung tip progenitor cell self-renewal (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observation shown in the referenced figure.

claim: SOX2 is not crucial for human foetal lung tip progenitor cell self-renewal.
source: SOX2 KO colonies proliferate and grow normally for at least four serial passages, suggesting that SOX2 is not crucial for human foetal lung tip progenitor cell self-renewal (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SOX2 KO organoids grow normally.

claim: The Organoid Easytag workflow was successfully applied to the human foetal intestinal organoid system to generate SOX9 reporter lines (2/4 lines tested correctly targeted).
source: Additionally, we tested the Organoid Easytag workflow in the human foetal intestinal organoid system (Elmentaite et al., 2020) and successfully derived SOX9 reporter lines (Figure 2e and f; 2/4 lines tested correctly targeted).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The Organoid Easytag pipeline can target various loci, including highly abundant genes, transcription factors, the human safe harbour locus and transcriptionally silent genes.
source: We have demonstrated that our Organoid Easytag pipeline can target various loci, including highly abundant genes, transcription factors, the human safe harbour locus and transcriptionally silent genes.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the various targeting experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Organoid Easytag can be adapted to generate KOs and applied to different organoid systems.
source: The Organoid Easytag workflow can also be adapted to generate KOs and applied to different organoid systems (efficiency details summarised in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SOX2 KO and intestinal organoid experiments.

claim: Organoid Easytag will be a complementary technique to the recently published CRISPR-HOT approach.
source: Organoid Easytag will be a complementary technique to the recently published CRISPR-HOT approach (Artegiani et al., 2020) and is particularly suited for experiments where precise gene editing is required (Figure 2—figure supplement 5f).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the utility of the method relative to another published approach.

claim: Organoid Easytag is particularly suited for experiments where precise gene editing is required.
source: Organoid Easytag will be a complementary technique to the recently published CRISPR-HOT approach (Artegiani et al., 2020) and is particularly suited for experiments where precise gene editing is required (Figure 2—figure supplement 5f).
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the method based on its design.

claim: KOs are not suitable for studying the function of genes which are required for stem cell self-renewal.
source: KOs are not suitable for studying the function of genes which are required for stem cell self-renewal.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of KO approaches based on established knowledge.

claim: Temporal and reversible control of gene expression cannot be easily achieved using KOs.
source: Moreover, temporal, and reversible, control of gene expression cannot be easily achieved using KOs.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of KO approaches based on established knowledge.

claim: Inducible CRISPRi could potentially solve the problems of studying genes required for self-renewal and achieving temporal control.
source: Inducible CRISPRi could potentially solve these problems.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement about the potential advantages of CRISPRi.

claim: The TetON system alone did not provide sufficiently tight control of CRISPRi, possibly due to copy number or integration position of the transgene.
source: However, the TetON system alone did not provide sufficiently tight control of CRISPRi, possibly due to copy number or integration position of the transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure, with speculation about the cause.

claim: The authors fused KRAB-dCas9 with a destabilising domain derived from Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) to solve the problem of leaky CRISPRi.
source: To solve this problem, we fused KRAB-dCas9 with a destabilising domain derived from Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described by the authors.

claim: DHFR is stabilised by a small molecule, trimethoprim (TMP).
source: DHFR is stabilised by a small molecule, trimethoprim (TMP) (Figure 3b; Iwamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: CD71 protein was depleted in the majority of cells (91.4% ± 2.1%, mean ± SEM, N = 3) after 5 days of Dox and TMP treatment using the inducible CRISPRi system.
source: Using previously validated gRNAs (Horlbeck et al., 2016), CD71 protein was depleted in the majority of the cells after 5 days of Dox and TMP treatment (91.4% ± 2.1%, mean ± SEM, N = 3; Figure 3c and d; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: No CD71 knockdown was observed in the no Dox/TMP treatment group, or in organoids transduced with non-targeting control gRNA.
source: Whereas no knockdown was observed in the no Dox/TMP treatment group, or in organoids transduced with non-targeting control gRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data serving as negative controls.

claim: The CD71 knockdown effect was achieved after 5 days, could be reversed after 1–2 weeks of Dox and TMP removal and then induced again.
source: The knockdown effect was achieved after 5 days, could be reversed after 1–2 weeks of Dox and TMP removal and then induced again (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c), consistent with a recent report (Nuñez et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figures and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: SOX2 could be efficiently knocked down at both the transcriptional and protein level using the inducible CRISPRi system.
source: We further evaluated the inducible CRISPRi system using SOX2. SOX2 could be efficiently knocked down at both the transcriptional and protein level and no background CRISPRi function was observed (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR and western blot data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: No background CRISPRi function was observed in the SOX2 knockdown experiments.
source: We further evaluated the inducible CRISPRi system using SOX2. SOX2 could be efficiently knocked down at both the transcriptional and protein level and no background CRISPRi function was observed (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no knockdown without induction.

claim: The SOX2 knockdown occurred by day 1 and was reversible.
source: The SOX2 knockdown occurred by day 1 and was also reversible (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), indicating that the CRISPRi function is efficient and tightly regulated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in the referenced figure.

claim: The CRISPRi function is efficient and tightly regulated.
source: The SOX2 knockdown occurred by day 1 and was also reversible (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d), indicating that the CRISPRi function is efficient and tightly regulated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics and reversibility data.

claim: No effects on organoid morphology or growth were observed after SOX2 knockdown.
source: Consistent with our SOX2 KO, we did not observe effects on organoid morphology or growth after SOX2 knockdown (Figure 3g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The SOX2 knockdown results further confirmed the finding that SOX2 is not crucial for organoid self-renewal.
source: Consistent with our SOX2 KO, we did not observe effects on organoid morphology or growth after SOX2 knockdown (Figure 3g and h). This further confirmed our finding that SOX2 is not crucial for organoid self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency between KO and knockdown results.

claim: The authors tested a previously reported CRISPRa system, dxCas9(3.7)-VPR, for its ability to activate SFTPC transcription.
source: We tested a previously reported CRISPRa system, dxCas9(3.7)-VPR (Hu et al., 2018), for its ability to activate SFTPC transcription (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a methodological approach described by the authors, citing the source of the CRISPRa system.

claim: Inducible CRISPRa can induce SFTPC gene expression efficiently at both transcriptional and protein level without influencing organoid growth.
source: Inducible CRISPRa can induce SFTPC gene expression efficiently at both transcriptional and protein level without influencing organoid growth (Figure 4b–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and microscopy data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: The authors have established a complete organoid genetic toolbox for gene targeting, reporter generation, controllable gene KOs, inducible gene knockdown and gene activation in the human foetal lung organoid system.
source: We have established a complete organoid genetic toolbox for gene targeting, reporter generation, controllable gene KOs, inducible gene knockdown and gene activation in the human foetal lung organoid system (efficiency details provided in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: These tools can be easily adapted for organoid systems derived from other tissues that are suitable to be nucleofected, or transduced by lentivirus.
source: We envision that these tools can be easily adapted for organoid systems derived from other tissues that are suitable to be nucleofected, or transduced by lentivirus.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the methods, supported by the successful application to intestinal organoids.

claim: These tools will empower tissue-derived organoids to model human congenital lung disease and benchmark gene function using the Human Cell Atlas as a reference.
source: This will empower tissue-derived organoids to model human congenital lung disease and benchmark gene function using the Human Cell Atlas as a reference.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential applications of the developed tools.
